records.our_prose: Jalapeno is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Capsicum annuum), the most popular hot pepper in American gardens, grown for its firm, medium-hot pods. Its culture is that of any pepper, close to a bell: a heat-loving, self-fertile, transplant crop set into warm soil after frost, growing slowly until the ground is truly warm, then bearing continuously through the summer. What sets it apart is pungency. Jalapeno carries capsaicin, roughly 2,500 to 8,000 Scoville units, produced in glands on the placenta inside the pod, and its heat is not fixed: it rises as the fruit ripens from green to red and as the plant meets stress, especially heat and a controlled water pull, so the same variety can be mild or fiery depending on how and when it is grown and picked. Two jalapeno-specific points reassure new growers: corking, the fine tan netting on a mature pod's skin, is a prized sign of quality, not a defect; and pods can be picked firm and dark green (the usual harvest, around 70 to 80 days from transplant) or left to ripen red for more heat and sweetness. Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and pauses fruit set when days climb above about 90°F and nights above 75°F, so in the hottest regions the crop splits into a spring and a fall flush around the peak of summer. Its pests are aphids (and the mosaic viruses they carry), flea beetles on seedlings, the pepper maggot (which largely spares thin-walled hot types), the pepper weevil in the South, and hornworms; its main diseases are bacterial spot, mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, and anthracnose, all held off by clean seed, rotation, warm well-drained soil, and dry foliage. Handle the harvest with gloves: capsaicin is an oil that burns skin and eyes.

records.our_prose: Jalapeno is a moderate feeder, not a heavy one. Follow a soil test, or work a modest amount of a balanced-to-low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen once the first fruits have set, about three to four weeks after planting, and again during harvest. Hold the nitrogen back before fruit set: too much early on drives a big leafy plant with few flowers, the single most common reason a pepper looks lush but sets almost no pods. Pair feeding with steady moisture, and note that a mild, deliberate water and nitrogen pull as the crop ripens tends to concentrate a hot pepper's heat.

records.our_prose: Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit when daytime highs pass about 90°F and, especially, when nighttime lows stay above 75°F, which UMD notes will slow or stop pod production. Across the Gulf and coastal plain, July and August bring exactly that combination of heat and warm nights (compounded by humidity and disease pressure), so fruit set pauses through the peak of summer. Growers therefore run a spring crop that sets before the heat and a fall crop as it eases, leaving midsummer paused. This pause reflects reduced fruit set at high temperature, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

records.our_prose: Jalapeno wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and like all peppers it grows slowly until the ground is truly warm. A sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay, since a pepper set into cold soil simply sits there until it heats up. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Steady, even moisture in a freely draining soil is the target: soggy roots stall the plant and invite the Phytophthora blight peppers are prone to, while a mild, deliberate water pull late in the season can actually sharpen a hot pepper's heat.

records.our_prose: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Peppers want steady, even moisture, and the water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set: swings from dry to soaked drop blossoms and cause blossom-end rot on the developing pods. Container plants dry out far faster and need closer attention. A note peculiar to hot peppers: a mild, deliberate water pull as the fruit ripens tends to raise the heat, so a hot pepper grown slightly lean and dry late in the season is often the hottest.
